headline: 🚨 Chocolate is toxic to dogs
action_text: Contact your vet or an emergency animal poison hotline immediately. Do not wait for symptoms — chocolate toxicity can be fatal and time matters.

headline: 🚨 Xylitol causes life-threatening low blood sugar in dogs
action_text: Go to an emergency vet NOW. Xylitol can cause rapid blood sugar drop and liver failure — this cannot wait.

headline: 🚨 Grapes and raisins can cause kidney failure
action_text: Contact your vet or emergency animal poison hotline now. Even small amounts can cause sudden kidney failure. Do not wait for symptoms.

headline: 🚨 Possible bloat (GDV) — this is life-threatening
action_text: Rush to an emergency vet NOW. Gastric dilation-volvulus (bloat) can be fatal within hours without surgery.

headline: 🚨 Immediate emergency
action_text: Call emergency vet services NOW or go to the nearest 24-hour animal hospital immediately.

negate_patterns: history of seizures and acting normal
headline: 🚨 Seizure — requires emergency care
action_text: Keep your dog safe from injury (clear furniture), do not restrain, time the seizure. Go to an emergency vet if the seizure lasts more than 2–3 minutes or if multiple seizures occur.

headline: 🚨 Onion and garlic are toxic to dogs
action_text: Contact your vet or animal poison hotline. Allium toxicity causes red blood cell damage that may not show for days. Cooking does not make it safe.

headline: 🚨 Macadamia nuts are toxic to dogs
action_text: Contact your vet now. Symptoms include weakness, vomiting, tremors, and fever. Usually not fatal but requires monitoring.

headline: ⚠️ Avocado can be harmful to dogs
action_text: Contact your vet. The flesh is mildly toxic; the pit is a choking/obstruction hazard and contains concentrated persin.

headline: 🚨 Alcohol is highly toxic to dogs
action_text: Contact your vet or emergency animal hotline immediately. Even small amounts can cause respiratory failure in dogs.

headline: 🚨 Breathing difficulty — go to emergency vet now
action_text: This is a life-threatening emergency. Blue or purple gums indicate oxygen deprivation. Go to the nearest emergency animal hospital immediately.

headline: 🚨 Trauma — emergency care needed
action_text: Go to an emergency vet immediately. Apply gentle pressure to any wounds with a clean cloth. Keep your dog as still and calm as possible during transport.

headline: 🚨 Eye proptosis — emergency
action_text: Cover the eye with a moist clean cloth and go to an emergency vet immediately. Do not try to push it back in.

headline: ⚠️ Repeated vomiting needs attention
action_text: If vomiting more than 2–3 times, or accompanied by lethargy, blood, or abdominal pain, see your vet today. Withhold food for 4–6 hours but keep water available.

headline: ⚠️ Blood in stool requires same-day vet visit
action_text: Small amounts of red blood can have minor causes, but it warrants a vet check today — especially if accompanied by vomiting or lethargy. Bright red blood is often lower GI; dark tarry stool can indicate upper GI bleeding (more serious).

headline: ⚠️ Possible foreign body ingestion
action_text: See your vet today. Swallowed objects can cause obstruction or perforation. Do not try to induce vomiting without vet guidance — some objects become more dangerous on the way up.

headline: ⚠️ Eye problems can deteriorate quickly
action_text: See a vet today. Eye injuries and infections worsen fast and can lead to permanent damage if untreated. Do not apply any eye drops without veterinary guidance.

headline: ⚠️ Possible allergic reaction
action_text: If your dog has facial swelling, difficulty breathing, or extreme lethargy after a sting or new exposure, go to an emergency vet NOW. Mild hives without breathing problems — see your vet today.

headline: ⚠️ Urinary issues need prompt attention
action_text: Inability to urinate is an emergency (blocked bladder). Blood in urine or painful urination warrants a same-day vet visit. Male dogs are at higher risk of full urinary blockage.

headline: ⚠️ Sudden inability to bear weight
action_text: Rest your dog and restrict movement. If non-weight-bearing on a limb or the leg looks deformed, see a vet today. This can indicate a fracture, ligament tear, or joint injury.

headline: 🚨 Suspected heat stroke — act immediately
action_text: Move to a cool area immediately, wet with cool (not cold) water, and fan. Go to an emergency vet now — heat stroke can be fatal rapidly.

headline: 💙 Mild limping — worth a vet check
action_text: Rest your dog and avoid strenuous activity. Schedule a vet appointment in the next few days. If the limp worsens, becomes non-weight-bearing, or is accompanied by swelling, move it up to urgent.

headline: 💙 Itching and scratching
action_text: Common causes include allergies, fleas, dry skin, or contact irritation. Schedule a vet visit if it's been more than a few days or you see skin changes, hair loss, or hotspots.

headline: 💙 Single vomiting episode — usually not serious
action_text: A single vomit, especially after eating grass, is often normal. Withhold food for 4–6 hours, then offer a small bland meal (rice + boiled chicken). Monitor for repeat vomiting, lethargy, or blood.

headline: 💙 Mild diarrhea — watch and manage
action_text: Offer a bland diet (boiled chicken and rice) for 24–48 hours. Keep water available to prevent dehydration. See a vet if it lasts more than 48 hours, or if your dog seems lethargic or stops eating.

headline: 💙 Possible ear infection
action_text: Schedule a vet visit this week. Ear infections are common and very treatable, but can worsen if left. Do not insert anything into the ear canal without vet guidance.

headline: 💙 Dental health check recommended
action_text: Bad breath in dogs is often a sign of periodontal disease. Schedule a dental examination. Regular brushing and dental chews can help prevent buildup.

headline: 💙 Weight management
action_text: Obesity is the most common preventable health problem in dogs. Use the Nutrition module to generate a feeding plan based on your dog's ideal weight. Schedule a vet visit to rule out thyroid or other metabolic conditions.

headline: ⚠️ Broken tooth — see vet this week
action_text: A cracked or broken tooth is painful and can lead to infection. Avoid hard chews on that side. Schedule a dental appointment this week.

headline: ℹ️ Puppy eating habits
action_text: New puppies often take 1–3 days to settle into eating in a new home. Offer meals 3–4 times daily at set times. If the puppy hasn't eaten in 24 hours or seems lethargic, see a vet. Stress, new environment, and food changes are common culprits.

headline: ℹ️ Puppies sleep 16–18 hours a day — that's normal
action_text: Young puppies need a lot of sleep for brain and body development. This is entirely normal as long as the puppy is eating, has normal stool, and is energetic when awake.

headline: 💙 Scooting often means anal glands need expressing
action_text: The most common cause is full or impacted anal glands. Schedule a vet or groomer appointment. Recurring scooting may indicate food allergy or worms.

headline: 💙 Cough — most often kennel cough
action_text: A honking or goose-like cough is often kennel cough (bordetella), which is usually self-limiting. Schedule a vet visit if it has persisted more than 5–7 days, is accompanied by fever or lethargy, or if your dog is very young or immunocompromised.

headline: 💙 Excessive thirst and urination
action_text: Polydipsia/polyuria can indicate diabetes, Cushing's disease, kidney disease, or Addison's — all manageable when caught early. Schedule a vet appointment and request blood and urine tests.

headline: ℹ️ Aggression — rule out pain first
action_text: Sudden aggression in a previously gentle dog is often pain-related. Schedule a vet visit to rule out injury or illness. If behavioral, a certified dog trainer or veterinary behaviorist can help. Never punish growling — it's communication.

headline: 💙 New lump — have it checked
action_text: Most lumps in dogs are benign (lipomas, cysts), but new growths should be examined by a vet. Note the size and location, and monitor for rapid changes.

headline: ⚠️ Rapidly changing mass — see vet soon
action_text: A lump that is growing quickly, changing color, ulcerating, or bleeding warrants a vet visit this week for examination and possible fine needle aspirate.

headline: 💙 Lethargy — watch for 24 hours
action_text: One quiet day after exercise or excitement is normal. If lethargy persists more than 24–48 hours, is accompanied by vomiting, diarrhea, or appetite loss, or comes on suddenly, schedule a vet visit.

headline: 💙 Appetite loss
action_text: A dog skipping one meal is usually not alarming. If appetite loss persists more than 48 hours or is accompanied by other symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy), see your vet.

headline: ⚠️ Not eating plus other symptoms
action_text: Appetite loss combined with vomiting, lethargy, or refusing water for more than 24 hours warrants a same-day vet visit to rule out obstruction, illness, or pain.
